engine: markdown
title: "Pipelines"
---

```{term}
#| include: false
rush run -o mtcars.csv 'mtcars'
```

The real power of `rush` is combining commands in Unix pipelines. `rush`
writes CSV when its output is piped, and reads standard input when you pass
`-` as the file. So it composes with other command-line tools, and with
itself.

## Chaining rush commands

Filter with `rush run`, then aggregate with SQL. Standard input is the
relation `stdin`:

```{term}
rush run 'dplyr::filter(df, cyl == 8)' mtcars.csv |
  rush sql "SELECT COUNT(*) AS n, ROUND(AVG(mpg), 1) AS avg_mpg FROM stdin" -
```

Or the other way around, and as many steps as you like:

```{term}
rush sql "SELECT mpg, cyl, hp, wt FROM mtcars WHERE hp > 200" mtcars.csv |
  rush run 'dplyr::arrange(df, mpg)' - |
  rush run 'head(df, 3)' -
```

## Changing formats along the way

Each step can use another format, as long as the next step knows which one it
reads (`-F`):

```{term}
rush run -O json 'head(df[1:4], 2)' mtcars.csv |
  rush run -F json 'dplyr::mutate(df, kpl = mpg * 0.425)' -
```

## Ending with a plot

`rush plot` also reads standard input when you pass `-`, so a pipeline can end
with a plot:

```{term}
rush sql "SELECT * FROM mtcars WHERE am = 1" mtcars.csv |
  rush plot -x wt -y mpg -O ascii -w 60 -
```

## With other tools

Use other tools before or after `rush`. For example, count the rows with
`wc` (without the header):

```{term}
rush run --no-output-header 'dplyr::filter(df, hp > 100)' mtcars.csv | wc -l
```

Or download JSON with `curl`, and summarize it. Note that the column names
are cleaned, so `Origin` becomes `origin`:

```{term}
curl -s https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/vega-datasets@2.11.0/data/cars.json |
  rush run -F json 'dplyr::count(df, origin)' -
```

```{term}
#| include: false
rm -f mtcars.csv
```
